source_refs.note: Book p. 73-76: 3.1.2 table of 15 derivatives and the indefinite integrals they give; Examples 1-12 (power rule, sums, General Power Rule, trigonometric integrals, exponential base a/b).

blocks.text: From (the above Definitions), we obtain integration formulas directly from differentiation formulas, as shown in the following table.

blocks.caption: Derivatives and the indefinite integrals they give (the book's table; it has no caption)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to use the table: each right-hand entry is the left-hand derivative read backwards. If you know the derivatives, you know these integrals.
Watch the signs: since \(\frac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x\), we get \(\int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x + c\). The same happens for \(\csc^{2}x\) and \(\csc x\cot x\).
Why \(\ln|x|\) and not \(\ln x\)? For \(x < 0\), \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln(-x) = \frac{-1}{-x} = \frac{1}{x}\) as well, so \(\ln|x|\) works on both sides of 0.
For \(a^{x}\) we divide by \(\ln a\), because differentiating \(a^{x}\) multiplies by \(\ln a\). For \(e^{x}\), \(\ln e = 1\), so nothing changes.
With Rule 5 every row also works for \(ax + b\) in place of \(x\): for example \(\int \sec^{2}(3x)\,dx = \frac{\tan 3x}{3} + c\).
\(\tan x\), \(\sec x\), \(\tan^{2}x\), \(\cos^{2}x\) are not in the table. Examples 5 to 9 show how to reach them with Rule 4 and trigonometric identities.

blocks.title: Example 1
steps:
Given: (i) the integrand \(x^{99}\); (ii) the integrand \(-98x^{-99}\).
To find: the indefinite integral of each.
Method: both are powers of \(x\), so the power rule (Rule 3) fits, since \(99 \ne -1\) and \(-99 \ne -1\). In (ii) the constant \(-98\) is first taken out by Rule 1.

(i) Apply the power rule with \(n = 99\)
\[\int x^{99}\,dx = \dfrac{x^{99+1}}{99+1} + c\]
\[= \dfrac{x^{100}}{100} + c\]
Why: Rule 3: add 1 to the power and divide by the new power.

(i) Verify by differentiation
The book writes: \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x^{100}}{100} + c\right) = \frac{100x^{99}}{100} + c = x^{99} + c\)
The derivative of the constant \(c\) is 0, so correctly:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^{100}}{100} + c\right) = \dfrac{100x^{99}}{100}\]
\[= x^{99}\]
Why: an antiderivative is confirmed when its derivative gives back the integrand.

(ii) Take the constant out
\[\int -98x^{-99}\,dx = -98\int x^{-99}\,dx\]
Why: Rule 1: a constant factor comes out of the integral.

(ii) Apply the power rule with \(n = -99\)
\[= -98\cdot\dfrac{x^{-98}}{-98} + c\]
\[= x^{-98} + c\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{x^{98}} + c\]
Why: \(-99 + 1 = -98\); the \(-98\) in front cancels the \(-98\) in the denominator; \(x^{-98} = \frac{1}{x^{98}}\).

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^{-98}\right) = -98x^{-99}\]
This is the integrand of (ii), and the derivative of \(\frac{x^{100}}{100}\) is \(x^{99}\), the integrand of (i).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Example 1(i): the book's check line prints \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x^{100}}{100} + c\right) = \frac{100x^{99}}{100} + c = x^{99} + c\). The derivative of the constant \(c\) is 0, so the line should read \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x^{100}}{100} + c\right) = \frac{100x^{99}}{100} = x^{99}\), with no \(+\,c\) after differentiating. The answer \(\frac{x^{100}}{100} + c\) itself is correct.

blocks.title: Example 2
steps:
Given: a polynomial integrand of five terms.
To find: its indefinite integral.
Method: Rule 2 splits it into five integrals, Rule 1 takes out the constants, and Rule 3 integrates each power.

Split term by term (Rule 2)
\[= \int 8x^{7}dx - \int 6x^{5}dx + \int 4x^{3}dx\]
\[\quad - \int 2x\,dx - \int 3\,dx\]
Why: the integral of a sum or difference is the sum or difference of the integrals.

Take the constants out (Rule 1)
\[= 8\int x^{7}dx - 6\int x^{5}dx + 4\int x^{3}dx\]
\[\quad - 2\int x\,dx - 3\int 1\,dx\]
Why: numbers multiplying a function come out of the integral.

Integrate each power (Rule 3)
\[= 8\left(\dfrac{x^{8}}{8}\right) - 6\left(\dfrac{x^{6}}{6}\right) + 4\left(\dfrac{x^{4}}{4}\right)\]
\[\quad - 2\left(\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right) - 3x + c\]
Why: add 1 to each power and divide by the new power; \(\int 1\,dx = x\). One constant \(c\) collects the constants of all five integrals.

Simplify
\[= x^{8} - x^{6} + x^{4} - x^{2} - 3x + c\]
Why: each coefficient cancels with the new power (\(\frac{8}{8} = 1\), \(\frac{6}{6} = 1\), and so on).

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{8} - x^{6} + x^{4} - x^{2} - 3x)\]
\[= 8x^{7} - 6x^{5} + 4x^{3} - 2x - 3\]
which is the integrand.

blocks.title: Example 3
steps:
Given: (i) \(\frac{7}{\sqrt{x}}\); (ii) \(\frac{(1+x^{2})^{2}}{x^{4}}\).
To find: both indefinite integrals.
Method: there is no rule for a quotient directly, so first rewrite each integrand as powers of \(x\); then use Rules 1, 2 and 3.

(i) Write the root as a power
\[\int \dfrac{7}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx = 7\int x^{-1/2}\,dx\]
Why: \(\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}\), so \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = x^{-1/2}\); the 7 comes out by Rule 1.

(i) Apply the power rule with \(n = -\frac{1}{2}\)
\[= 7\,\dfrac{x^{1/2}}{1/2} + c\]
\[= 14\sqrt{x} + c\]
Why: \(-\frac{1}{2} + 1 = \frac{1}{2}\); dividing by \(\frac{1}{2}\) means multiplying by 2.

(ii) Expand the numerator
\[\int \dfrac{(1+x^{2})^{2}}{x^{4}}\,dx = \int \dfrac{1 + 2x^{2} + x^{4}}{x^{4}}\,dx\]
Why: \((a+b)^{2} = a^{2} + 2ab + b^{2}\). A bracket squared must be opened before dividing.

(ii) Divide each term by \(x^{4}\) (Rule 2)
\[= \int \left(\dfrac{1}{x^{4}} + \dfrac{2x^{2}}{x^{4}} + \dfrac{x^{4}}{x^{4}}\right)dx\]
\[= \int (x^{-4} + 2x^{-2} + 1)\,dx\]
Why: \(\frac{x^{m}}{x^{k}} = x^{m-k}\); now every term is a power of \(x\).

(ii) Integrate each term (Rule 3)
\[= \dfrac{x^{-3}}{-3} + 2\,\dfrac{x^{-1}}{-1} + x + c\]
\[= -\dfrac{1}{3x^{3}} - \dfrac{2}{x} + x + c\]
Why: \(-4 + 1 = -3\) and \(-2 + 1 = -1\); neither power is \(-1\) before integrating, so the power rule applies.

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(14x^{1/2}) = 7x^{-1/2} = \dfrac{7}{\sqrt{x}}\]
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-\tfrac{1}{3}x^{-3} - 2x^{-1} + x\right)\]
\[= x^{-4} + 2x^{-2} + 1\]
Both give back the integrands.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Examples 1 to 3 all follow one plan: first rewrite the integrand as a sum of powers of \(x\) (roots as fractional powers, divisions as negative powers, squares expanded), then apply Rules 1, 2 and 3. Example 4 shows the General Power Rule, where a bracket is treated like a single \(x\).

blocks.title: Example 4
steps:
Given: two integrals with their results printed in the book (no working is printed).
To show: why each result is true.
Method: in each integrand a bracket is raised to a power and multiplied by the derivative of that bracket, so the General Power Rule applies.

(i) Identify \(f(x)\), \(f'(x)\) and \(n\)
\[f(x) = 5x^{2} + 7x - 3\]
\[f'(x) = 10x + 7,\quad n = 7\]
Why: the factor \((10x + 7)\) beside the bracket is exactly the derivative of the bracket.

(i) Apply the General Power Rule
\[\int [f(x)]^{7} f'(x)\,dx = \dfrac{[f(x)]^{8}}{8} + c\]
\[= \dfrac{(5x^{2} + 7x - 3)^{8}}{8} + c\]
Why: treat the whole bracket like \(x\) in the power rule: add 1 to the power, divide by the new power.

(ii) Identify \(f(x)\), \(f'(x)\) and \(n\)
\[f(x) = x + \dfrac{1}{x}\]
\[f'(x) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{x^{2}},\quad n = 1\]
Why: \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^{-1}) = -x^{-2} = -\frac{1}{x^{2}}\), so the second bracket is the derivative of the first.

(ii) Apply the General Power Rule
\[\int f(x)\,f'(x)\,dx = \dfrac{[f(x)]^{2}}{2} + c\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(x + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)^{2} + c\]
Why: \(n = 1\), so the new power is 2.

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\dfrac{(5x^{2}+7x-3)^{8}}{8}\]
\[= (5x^{2}+7x-3)^{7}(10x+7)\]
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\,\dfrac{1}{2}\left(x + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)^{2}\]
\[= \left(x + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right)\]
(chain rule). Both results are confirmed.

blocks.title: Example 5
steps:
Given: the integrand \(\tan x\).
To find: \(\int \tan x\,dx\).
Method: \(\tan x\) is not in the table. Multiply and divide by \(\sec x\) so that the numerator becomes the derivative of the denominator; then Rule 4 applies.

Multiply and divide by \(\sec x\)
\[\int \tan x\,dx = \int \dfrac{\sec x \cdot \tan x}{\sec x}\,dx\]
Why: \(\frac{\sec x}{\sec x} = 1\) does not change the value, and \(\frac{d}{dx}(\sec x) = \sec x\tan x\) is now on top.

Apply Rule 4
\[= \ln|\sec x| + c\]
Why: \(\int \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx = \ln|f(x)| + c\) with \(f(x) = \sec x\).

The other form
\[\ln|\sec x| = \ln\left|\dfrac{1}{\cos x}\right| = -\ln|\cos x|\]
\[\text{or}\quad = -\ln|\cos x| + c\]
Why: \(\ln\frac{1}{u} = -\ln u\). Both forms are correct.

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(-\ln|\cos x|) = -\dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x}\]
\[= \tan x\]
blocks.answer: \(\int \tan x\,dx = \ln|\sec x| + c\), or \(-\ln|\cos x| + c\)

blocks.title: Example 6
steps:
Given: the integrand \(\sec x\).
To find: \(\int \sec x\,dx\).
Method: a standard trick: multiply and divide by \(\sec x + \tan x\). The new numerator is then the derivative of the new denominator, so Rule 4 applies.

Multiply and divide by \(\sec x + \tan x\)
\[\int \sec x\,dx = \int \dfrac{\sec x(\sec x + \tan x)}{(\sec x + \tan x)}\,dx\]
Why: multiplying by \(\frac{\sec x + \tan x}{\sec x + \tan x} = 1\) keeps the value.

Open the bracket and rearrange
\[= \int \dfrac{\sec^{2}x + \sec x\tan x}{\sec x + \tan x}\,dx\]
\[= \int \dfrac{\sec x\tan x + \sec^{2}x}{\sec x + \tan x}\,dx\]
Why: \(\frac{d}{dx}(\sec x + \tan x) = \sec x\tan x + \sec^{2}x\), which is exactly the numerator.

Apply Rule 4
The book's last line: \(= -\ln|\cos x| + c\) (By Rule 4)
Correctly, Rule 4 with \(f(x) = \sec x + \tan x\) gives:
\[= \ln|\sec x + \tan x| + c\]
Why: \(\int \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx = \ln|f(x)| + c\), and here \(f(x)\) is the denominator \(\sec x + \tan x\).

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln|\sec x + \tan x|\]
\[= \dfrac{\sec x\tan x + \sec^{2}x}{\sec x + \tan x}\]
\[= \dfrac{\sec x(\tan x + \sec x)}{\sec x + \tan x} = \sec x\]
The printed \(-\ln|\cos x|\) instead differentiates to \(\tan x\) (Example 5), not \(\sec x\).
blocks.answer: \(\int \sec x\,dx = \ln|\sec x + \tan x| + c\) (the book's last line \(-\ln|\cos x| + c\) is wrong; see the Book correction)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Example 6: the book's solution ends with \(\int \sec x\,dx = -\ln|\cos x| + c\) (By Rule 4). That is the answer of Example 5 (\(\int \tan x\,dx\)); its derivative is \(\tan x\), not \(\sec x\). The numerator \(\sec x\tan x + \sec^{2}x\) is the derivative of the denominator \(\sec x + \tan x\), so Rule 4 gives \(\int \sec x\,dx = \ln|\sec x + \tan x| + c\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Examples 5 to 11 show the main ideas for trigonometric integrals: make the numerator the derivative of the denominator (Rule 4: Examples 5, 6, 11), replace powers by identities (\(\tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x - 1\), \(\cos^{2}x = \frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}\): Examples 7, 8), rewrite in \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) (Example 9), and turn products into sums (Example 10).

blocks.title: Example 7
steps:
Given: the integrand \(\tan^{2}x\).
To find: \(\int \tan^{2}x\,dx\).
Method: \(\tan^{2}x\) is not in the table, but \(\sec^{2}x\) is. The identity \(1 + \tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x\) changes one into the other.

Use the identity
\[\int \tan^{2}x\,dx = \int (\sec^{2}x - 1)\,dx\]
Why: from \(1 + \tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x\) we get \(\tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x - 1\).

Split and integrate (Rule 2 and the table)
\[= \int \sec^{2}x\,dx - \int 1\,dx\]
\[= \tan x - x + c\]
Why: \(\int \sec^{2}x\,dx = \tan x\) and \(\int 1\,dx = x\).

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan x - x) = \sec^{2}x - 1 = \tan^{2}x\]

blocks.title: Example 8
steps:
Given: the integrand \(\cos^{2}x\).
To find: \(\int \cos^{2}x\,dx\).
Method: a square of cosine has no table formula. The double-angle identity \(\cos^{2}x = \frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}\) removes the square.

Use the identity
\[\int \cos^{2}x\,dx = \int \dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}\,dx\]
Why: \(\cos 2x = 2\cos^{2}x - 1\), so \(\cos^{2}x = \frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}\).

Take out \(\frac{1}{2}\) and integrate
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\int (1 + \cos 2x)\,dx\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[x + \dfrac{\sin 2x}{2}\right] + c\]
Why: Rule 1 for \(\frac{1}{2}\); \(\int \cos 2x\,dx = \frac{\sin 2x}{2}\) by Rule 5 with \(a = 2\).

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{\sin 2x}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\cos 2x}{2}\]
\[= \dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2} = \cos^{2}x\]

blocks.title: Example 9
steps:
Given: \(\frac{\tan x - \sec x}{1 + \tan^{2}x}\).
To find: its indefinite integral.
Method: replace \(1 + \tan^{2}x\) by \(\sec^{2}x\), split the fraction, and write everything in \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\).

Use \(1 + \tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x\) and split
\[= \int \dfrac{\tan x - \sec x}{\sec^{2}x}\,dx\]
\[= \int \left(\dfrac{\tan x}{\sec^{2}x} - \dfrac{\sec x}{\sec^{2}x}\right)dx\]
Why: a fraction with a difference on top splits into two fractions with the same denominator.

Write in \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\)
\[= \int \left(\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\cos^{2}x - \dfrac{1}{\sec x}\right)dx\]
\[= \int (\sin x\cos x - \cos x)\,dx\]
Why: \(\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\) and \(\frac{1}{\sec^{2}x} = \cos^{2}x\); \(\frac{\sec x}{\sec^{2}x} = \frac{1}{\sec x} = \cos x\).

Integrate
\[= \dfrac{\sin^{2}x}{2} - \sin x + c\]
Why: in \(\int \sin x\cos x\,dx\), \(\cos x\) is the derivative of \(\sin x\), so the General Power Rule (with \(n = 1\)) gives \(\frac{\sin^{2}x}{2}\); and \(\int \cos x\,dx = \sin x\).

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\sin^{2}x}{2} - \sin x\right)\]
\[= \sin x\cos x - \cos x\]
which is the simplified integrand.

blocks.title: Example 10
steps:
Given: a product \(\sin 3x\cos 7x\).
To find: its indefinite integral.
Method: there is no rule for a product, so change it into a sum by the product-to-sum formula, then integrate each sine by Rule 5.

The formula
\[\sin mx\cos nx\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}[\sin(m+n)x + \sin(m-n)x]\]
Why: it turns a product into a sum, which Rule 2 can split.

Put \(m = 3\) and \(n = 7\)
\[\int \sin 3x\cos 7x\,dx\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\int [\sin(10x) + \sin(-4x)]\,dx\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\int (\sin 10x - \sin 4x)\,dx\]
Why: \(3 + 7 = 10\), \(3 - 7 = -4\), and \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\).

Integrate each term (Rule 5)
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[-\dfrac{\cos 10x}{10} - \left(-\dfrac{\cos 4x}{4}\right)\right] + c\]
\[= -\dfrac{\cos 10x}{20} + \dfrac{\cos 4x}{8} + c\]
Why: \(\int \sin ax\,dx = -\frac{\cos ax}{a}\).

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-\dfrac{\cos 10x}{20} + \dfrac{\cos 4x}{8}\right)\]
\[= \dfrac{\sin 10x}{2} - \dfrac{\sin 4x}{2}\]
which equals \(\frac{1}{2}(\sin 10x - \sin 4x) = \sin 3x\cos 7x\).

blocks.title: Example 11
steps:
Given: \(\frac{\sin(x+a)}{\sin(x+b)}\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are constants.
To find: its indefinite integral.
Method: write the angle on top in terms of the angle below: \(x + a = (x + b) + (a - b)\). Expanding by the sine addition formula leaves terms we can integrate.

Rewrite the angle
\[\int \dfrac{\sin(x+a)}{\sin(x+b)}\,dx\]
\[= \int \dfrac{\sin[(x+b) + (a-b)]}{\sin(x+b)}\,dx\]
Why: \((x+b) + (a-b) = x + a\), so nothing changes, but now the denominator's angle appears on top.

Expand by \(\sin(A+B) = \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B\)
\[\sin[(x+b) + (a-b)]\]
\[= \sin(x+b)\cos(a-b)\]
\[\quad + \cos(x+b)\sin(a-b)\]
Why: \(A = x + b\), \(B = a - b\).

Divide by \(\sin(x+b)\)
\[= \int \left[\cos(a-b) + \sin(a-b)\dfrac{\cos(x+b)}{\sin(x+b)}\right]dx\]
\[= \cos(a-b)\int 1\,dx\]
\[\quad + \sin(a-b)\int \dfrac{\cos(x+b)}{\sin(x+b)}\,dx\]
Why: \(\cos(a-b)\) and \(\sin(a-b)\) contain no \(x\), so they are constants and come out by Rule 1.

Integrate
\[= \cos(a-b)\cdot x\]
\[\quad + \sin(a-b)\cdot\ln|\sin(x+b)| + c\]
Why: \(\cos(x+b)\) is the derivative of \(\sin(x+b)\), so Rule 4 gives \(\ln|\sin(x+b)|\).

Check:
Differentiating gives \(\cos(a-b) + \sin(a-b)\frac{\cos(x+b)}{\sin(x+b)}\); over the common denominator the numerator is \(\sin(x+b)\cos(a-b) + \cos(x+b)\sin(a-b) = \sin(x+a)\), so we get back \(\frac{\sin(x+a)}{\sin(x+b)}\).

blocks.title: Example 12
steps:
Given: \(\frac{a^{2x} - b^{2x}}{(ab)^{x}}\), with \(a, b > 0\) and \(a \ne b\) (so that \(\frac{a}{b}\) is a positive base other than 1).
To find: its indefinite integral.
Method: use the laws of exponents to write each term as a single power \(\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{x}\) or \(\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^{x}\); then use the table formula \(\int k^{x}\,dx = \frac{k^{x}}{\ln k} + c\).

Split the fraction
\[= \int \dfrac{a^{2x} - b^{2x}}{a^{x}b^{x}}\,dx\]
\[= \int \left[\dfrac{a^{2x}}{a^{x}b^{x}} - \dfrac{b^{2x}}{a^{x}b^{x}}\right]dx\]
Why: \((ab)^{x} = a^{x}b^{x}\).

Simplify the powers
\[= \int \left[\dfrac{a^{2x-x}}{b^{x}} - \dfrac{b^{2x-x}}{a^{x}}\right]dx\]
\[= \int \left[\dfrac{a^{x}}{b^{x}} - \dfrac{b^{x}}{a^{x}}\right]dx\]
Why: \(\frac{a^{2x}}{a^{x}} = a^{2x-x} = a^{x}\), and the same for \(b\).

Write as single powers
\[= \int \left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^{x}dx - \int \left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)^{x}dx\]
Why: \(\frac{a^{x}}{b^{x}} = \left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{x}\); Rule 2 splits the difference.

Apply \(\int k^{x}\,dx = \frac{k^{x}}{\ln k} + c\)
\[= \dfrac{\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{x}}{\ln\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)} - \dfrac{\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^{x}}{\ln\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)} + c\]
Why: the table row for \(a^{x}\), used once with base \(\frac{a}{b}\) and once with base \(\frac{b}{a}\).

Check:
\(\frac{d}{dx}\frac{k^{x}}{\ln k} = k^{x}\), so the derivative is \(\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{x} - \left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^{x} = \frac{a^{2x} - b^{2x}}{(ab)^{x}}\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Results worth learning by heart from this page: \(\int \tan x\,dx = \ln|\sec x| + c\), \(\int \sec x\,dx = \ln|\sec x + \tan x| + c\), \(\int \tan^{2}x\,dx = \tan x - x + c\), \(\int \cos^{2}x\,dx = \frac{x}{2} + \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + c\). In the same way \(\int \cot x\,dx = \ln|\sin x| + c\) and \(\int \sin^{2}x\,dx = \frac{x}{2} - \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + c\) (our additions; check them by differentiating).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Every derivative formula read backwards is an integral formula; learn the table together with the derivatives.
2. Rewrite first, integrate second: powers for roots and fractions, identities for squares of trigonometric functions, product-to-sum for products.
3. If the numerator is the derivative of the denominator, the answer is \(\ln|\text{denominator}| + c\) (Rule 4).
4. \(\int a^{x}\,dx = \frac{a^{x}}{\ln a} + c\): the variable is in the exponent, so the power rule does not apply.
5. Check every answer by differentiating; one constant \(c\) is enough for the whole answer.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Sign errors: \(\int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x + c\), \(\int \csc^{2}x\,dx = -\cot x + c\).
2. Treating a power of a trigonometric function like a power of \(x\): \(\int \tan^{2}x\,dx \ne \frac{\tan^{3}x}{3} + c\).
3. Forgetting to divide by \(a\) for \(ax\) inside: \(\int \cos 2x\,dx = \frac{\sin 2x}{2} + c\), not \(\sin 2x + c\).
4. Using the power rule on \(a^{x}\): \(\int 2^{x}\,dx = \frac{2^{x}}{\ln 2} + c\), not \(\frac{2^{x+1}}{x+1}\).
5. Writing \(+\,c\) after differentiating in a check (the book itself does this in Example 1).
